Developments in 
Cisco IOS Forensics

Felix ‘FX’ Lindner
BlackHat Briefings
Washington DC, Feb. 2008

 Agenda

(cid:131) IP Routing Infrastructure and Cisco IOS
(cid:131) Cisco IOS Internals
(cid:131) Debugging and Post Mortem Analysis Today
(cid:131) A New Analysis Approach

(cid:131) Proposal
(cid:131) Features
(cid:131) Challenges

(cid:131) Initial Public Offer
(cid:131) Future Work

 IP Routing Infrastructure

(cid:131) The Internet and corporate networks almost 

exclusively run on the Internet Protocol
(cid:131) IP Version 4 is still prevalent protocol
(cid:131) IP Version 6 coming up very slowly

(cid:131) The design of IP requires intelligent nodes in 

the network to make routing decisions
(cid:131) This is a design principle of the protocol and 

cannot be changed

(cid:131) “Flat” networks have their own issues

 IP Infrastructure & Security

(cid:131) All security protocols on top of IP share 

common design goals:
(cid:131) Guarantee end-to-end integrity (some also 

confidentiality) of the traffic

(cid:131) Detect modification, replay, injection and holding 

back of traffic

(cid:131) Inform the upper protocol layers

(cid:131) None of them can recover from attacks rooted 

in the routing infrastructure
(cid:131) Security protocols cannot influence routing

 Infrastructure Monoculture

(cid:131) Cisco Systems’ routing platforms form the single 
largest population of networking equipment today
(cid:131) Equivalently distributed in the Internet core, government 

and corporate networks

(cid:131) Many different hardware platforms with different CPUs
(cid:131) Large investment sums bound to the equipment
(cid:131) Hard to replace
(cid:131) All run basically the same operating system

(cid:131) Protecting this infrastructure is critical
(cid:131) Therefore, in-depth analysis and diagnostics are of 

paramount importance

 Cisco IOS

(cid:131) Cisco® Internetwork Operating System®
(cid:131) Monolithic operating system
(cid:131) Compile-time linked functionality –

the 3 dimensional complexity of IOS
(cid:131) Platform dependent code
(cid:131) Feature-set dependent code
(cid:131) Major, Minor and Release version dependent code
(cid:131) Several tens of thousands different IOS images 

used in today’s networks
(cid:131) Over 10.000 still officially supported 

 Inside Cisco IOS

(cid:131) One large ELF binary
(cid:131) Essentially a large, statically linked UNIX 

program
(cid:131) Loaded by ROMMON, a kind-of BIOS
(cid:131) Runs directly on the router’s main CPU

(cid:131) If the CPU provides virtual memory and privilege 
separation (for example Supervisor and User 
mode on MIPS), it will not be used

 Inside Cisco IOS

(cid:131) Processes are rather like threads

(cid:131) No virtual memory mapping per process

(cid:131) Run-to-completion, cooperative multitasking

(cid:131) Interrupt driven handling of critical events

(cid:131) System-wide global data structures 

(cid:131) Common heap
(cid:131) Very little abstraction around the data structures
(cid:131) No way to force abstraction

 The IOS Code Security Issue

(cid:131) 12.4(16a) with enterprise base feature set consists of 

25.316.780 bytes binary code!
(cid:131) This is a 2600 with PowerPC CPU
(cid:131) Not including 505.900 bytes firmware for E1T1 and 

initialization

(cid:131) All written in plain C
(cid:131) Sharing the same address space
(cid:131) Sharing the same heap
(cid:131) Sharing the same data structures
(cid:131) Sharing millions of pointers

 The IOS Code Security Issue

(cid:131) A single mistake in the most unimportant 

piece of code can influence anything on the 
system, including kernel, security subsystems 
and cryptographic code.

(cid:131) Therefore, everything on IOS is a good target 
for remote code execution exploits in kernel 
context.

 Isn’t Cisco aware of that?

(cid:131) Cisco recently started the distribution of the next 

generation IOS-XR
(cid:131) Commercial QNX microkernel
(cid:131) Real processes (memory protection?)
(cid:131) Concurrent scheduling
(cid:131) Significantly higher hardware requirements

(cid:131) People never use the latest IOS

(cid:131) Production corporate networks usually run on 12.1 or 12.2, 

which 12.5 is already available

(cid:131) Not even Cisco’s own engineers would recommend the 

latest IOS release to a customer

(cid:131) That only covers people actively maintaining their 

network, not everyone running one

 Just, how often 
are routers hacked?
(cid:131) Keynote speaker Jerry Dixon mentioned not updated routers 

as a cause for concern
(cid:131) Do you know how expensive that is?

(cid:131) Old vulnerabilities like the HTTP level 16 bug are still actively 

scanned for
(cid:131) The router is used as a jump pad for further attacks

(cid:131) TCL backdoors are commonly used
(cid:131) Patched images are not rare
(cid:131) IOS images cost money
(cid:131) People will use images from anywhere
(cid:131) Patching images is not hard

(cid:131) Lawful Interception is its own can of worms

(cid:131) The router’s operator is not supposed to know that LI is performed
(cid:131) Who watches the watchers?

 And the future?

(cid:131) Ever noticed attackers take on the target with the 
lowest efforts required and the highest return of 
invest?
(cid:131) Windows became just a lot harder
(cid:131) UNIXes are hardened, even OS X
(cid:131) Infected PCs leave obvious traces

(cid:131) The question is not: 

“Will routers become a target?”

(cid:131) The question should be: 

“Do we want to know when they did?”

 Summary – Part I

(cid:131) A significant share of the Internet, 

governmental and corporate networks runs on:
(cid:131) one out of several tens of thousands of builds
(cid:131) of more or less the same code base
(cid:131) in a single process environment
... and we cannot bypass it, even if we could 
tell that it’s compromised

Next question: How can we even tell?

 Error Handling and Recovery

(cid:131) The software architecture of IOS dictates how 

exception handling has to be done
(cid:131) Remember, IOS is like a large UNIX process
(cid:131) What happens when a UNIX process segfaults?
(cid:131) Upon an exception, IOS can only restart the 

entire system
(cid:131) Even on-board, scheduled diagnostic processes 

can only forcefully crash the system

 Crash Cause Evidence

(cid:131) Reboot is a clean recovery method
(cid:131) Reboot destroys all volatile evidence of the 

crash cause
(cid:131) Everything on the router is volatile!
(cid:131) Exception: startup configuration and IOS image
(cid:131) Later IOS releases write an information file 

called “crashinfo”
(cid:131) Crashinfo contains very little information
(cid:131) Contents depend on what IOS thought was the 

cause of the crash

 Runtime Evidence

(cid:131) Crashinfo is only written upon device crashes
(cid:131) Successful attacks don’t cause device crashes
(cid:131) The available methods are:

(cid:131) Show commands
(cid:131) Debug commands
(cid:131) SNMP monitoring
(cid:131) Syslog monitoring

 Show Commands

(cid:131) IOS offers a plethora of inspection commands 

known as the “show” commands
(cid:131) Requires access to the command line interface

(cid:131) Geared towards network engineers
(cid:131) Thousands of different options and versions
(cid:131) Almost no access to code

(cid:131) 12.4 even limits memory show commands

 Debug Commands

(cid:131) “debug” enables in-code debugging output
(cid:131) Debug output has scheduler precedence
(cid:131) Too much debug output halts the router
(cid:131) Not an option in production environments 
(cid:131) Enabling the right debug output is an art

(cid:131) Turn on the wrong ones and you see very little
(cid:131) Turn on too many and the router stops working
(cid:131) Commands depend on the IOS version

(cid:131) For debug commands to be useful, you have to know 

what you are looking for before it happens
(cid:131) Not very useful for security analysis

 SNMP and Syslog Monitoring

(cid:131) Commonly accepted method for monitoring 

networking equipment

(cid:131) SNMP depending on the implemented MIB

(cid:131) Geared towards networking functionality
(cid:131) Very little process related information

(cid:131) Syslog is about as useful for security monitoring on 

IOS as it is on UNIX systems

(cid:131) Both generate continuous network traffic
(cid:131) Both consume system resources on the router
(cid:131) Then again, someone has to read the logs.

 Summary – Part II

(cid:131) Identifying compromised routers using today’s 
tools and methods is hard, if not impossible.
(cid:131) There is not enough data to perform any post 
mortem analysis of router crashes, security 
related or not.

(cid:131) We cannot distinguish between a functional 

problem, an attempted attack and a successful 
attack on infrastructure running IOS.

 A (not so) New Approach

(cid:131) We need the maximum amount of evidence
(cid:131) A full snapshot of the device is just enough

(cid:131) We don’t need it continuously

(cid:131) We need it on-demand 
(cid:131) We need it when the device crashes

(cid:131) We need an independent and solid analysis 

framework to process the evidence
(cid:131) We need to be able to extend and adjust it

 Getting the Evidence

(cid:131) Cisco IOS can write complete core dumps

(cid:131) Memory dump of the main memory
(cid:131) Memory dump of the IO memory
(cid:131) Memory dump of the PCI memory (if applicable)

(cid:131) Core dumps are written in two cases

(cid:131) The device crashes
(cid:131) The user issues the “write core” command

 Core Dump Destinations

(cid:131) IOS supports various destinations

(cid:131) TFTP server (bug!)
(cid:131) FTP server
(cid:131) RCP server
(cid:131) Flash file system (later IOS releases)

(cid:131) Core dumps are enabled by configuration

(cid:131) Configuration commands do not differ between 

IOS versions

(cid:131) Configuration change has no effect on the 

router’s operation or performance

 Core Dump 
Enabled Infrastructure

(cid:131) Configure all IOS devices to dump core onto 
one or more centrally located FTP servers
(cid:131) Minimizes required monitoring of devices: A router 
crashed if you find a core dump on the FTP server

(cid:131) Preserves evidence
(cid:131) Allows crash correlation between different routers

(cid:131) Why wasn’t it used before?

(cid:131) Core dumps were useless, except for Cisco 

developers and exploit writers.

 Analyzing Core Dumps

Disclaimer:

(cid:131) Any of the following methods can be 

implemented in whatever your preferred 
programming language is.

(cid:131) This presentation will be centric to our 
implementation: Recurity Labs CIR.

 Core Dump 
Analyzer Requirements

(cid:131) Must be 100% independent

(cid:131) No Cisco code
(cid:131) No disassembly based analysis
(cid:131) Must gradually recover abstraction
(cid:131) No assumptions about anything
(cid:131) Ability to cope with massively corrupted data

(cid:131) Should not be exploitable itself

(cid:131) Preferably not written in C

 The Image Blueprint

(cid:131) The IOS image (ELF file) contains all required 
information about the memory mapping on the 
router.
(cid:131) The image serves as the memory layout blueprint, 

to be applied to the core files

(cid:131) Using a known-to-be-good image also allows 
verification of the code and read-only data 
segments
(cid:131) Now we can easily and reliably detect runtime 

patched images

 Heap Reconstruction

(cid:131) IOS uses one large heap
(cid:131) The IOS heap contains plenty of meta-data for 

debugging purposes
(cid:131) 40 bytes overhead per heap block in IOS up to 

12.3

(cid:131) 48 bytes overhead per heap block in IOS 12.4

(cid:131) Reconstructing the entire heap allows 
extensive integrity and validity checks
(cid:131) Exceeding by far the on-board checks IOS 

performs during runtime

 Heap Verification

(cid:131) Full functionality of “CheckHeaps”

(cid:131) Verify the integrity of the allocated and free heap block 

doubly linked lists

(cid:131) Find holes in addressable heap

(cid:131) Invisible to CheckHeaps

(cid:131) Identify heap overflow footprints
(cid:131) Values not verified by CheckHeaps

(cid:131) Map heap blocks to referencing processes
(cid:131) Identify formerly allocated heap blocks

(cid:131) Catches memory usage peaks from the recent past

 Process List

(cid:131) Extraction of the IOS Process List
(cid:131) Identify the processes’ stack block

(cid:131) Create individual, per process back-traces
(cid:131) Identify return address overwrites

(cid:131) Obtain the processes’ scheduling state
(cid:131) Obtain the processes’ CPU usage history
(cid:131) Obtain the processes’ CPU context

(cid:131) Almost any post mortem analysis method 

known can be applied, given the two 
reconstructed data structures.

 TCL Backdoor Detection

(cid:131) TCL scripting is available on later Cisco IOS versions
(cid:131) TCL scripts listening on TCP sockets 

(cid:131) Well known method
(cid:131) Used to simplify automated administration
(cid:131) Used to silently keep privileged access to routers
(cid:131) Known bug: 

not terminated when the VTY session ends (fixed)

(cid:131) Simple TCL backdoor scripts published

(cid:131) CIR can extract all TCP script chunks from IOS heap 

and dump them for further analysis

 Your Wishes Please !

(cid:131) Interface tables
(cid:131) Static routing
(cid:131) Router processes
(cid:131) VLAN tables
(cid:131) VPN context

(cid:131) Keys
(cid:131) User
(cid:131) IPv6 tables
(cid:131) ARP tables
(cid:131) Dialer tables

(cid:131) CDP tables
(cid:131) Spanning tree
(cid:131) Access Lists
(cid:131) CEF Tree
(cid:131) User sessions
(cid:131) Listening ports

(cid:131) Callback code for 

incoming connections

(cid:131) Verification that it is 
located in .TEXT

 IOS Packet 
Forwarding Memory

(cid:131) IOS performs routing either as:

(cid:131) Process switching
(cid:131) Fast switching
(cid:131) Particle systems
(cid:131) Hardware accelerated switching

(cid:131) Except hardware switching, all use IO memory

(cid:131) IO memory is written as separate code dump
(cid:131) By default, about 6% of the router’s memory is dedicated 

as IO memory

(cid:131) In real world installations, it is common to increase the percentage 

to speed up forwarding

(cid:131) Hardware switched packets use PCI memory
(cid:131) PCI memory is written as separate core dump

 IO Memory Buffers

(cid:131) Routing (switching) ring buffers are grouped by 

packet size
(cid:131) Small
(cid:131) Medium
(cid:131) Big
(cid:131) Huge

(cid:131) Interfaces have their own buffers for locally handled 

traffic

(cid:131) IOS tries really hard to not copy packets around in 

memory

(cid:131) New traffic does not automatically erase older traffic 

in a linear way

 Traffic Extraction

(cid:131) CIR dumps packets that were process switched by 

the router from IO memory into a PCAP file
(cid:131) Traffic addressed to and from the router itself
(cid:131) Traffic that was process switching inspected

(cid:131) Access List matching
(cid:131) QoS routed traffic

(cid:131) CIR could dump packets that were forwarded 

through the router too
(cid:131) Reconstruction of packet fragments possible
(cid:131) Is it desirable?

 Advanced Traffic Extraction

(cid:131) Writing core to a remote server uses IO memory

(cid:131) Overwrites part of the traffic evidence

(cid:131) CIR can use a GDB link instead of a core dump

(cid:131) Serial GDB protocol allows direct access to router memory 

via the console

(cid:131) Uses Zynamics GDB debug link

(cid:131) Disconnecting all network interfaces preserves IO 

and PCI memory contents
(cid:131) Using GDB halts the router

(cid:131) All data is preserved – useful for emergency 

inspections

 Traffic Extraction Applications

(cid:131) Identification of attack jump pad routers
(cid:131) 0day identification against systems on 

segmented network interfaces
(cid:131) If you got the packet, you got the 0day

(cid:131) Spoofing attack backtracking
(cid:131) One hop at the time, obviously

(cid:131) LE detection

 Challenges

(cid:131) The analysis framework has to handle the complexity of the 

Cisco IOS landscape 
(cid:131) Hardware platforms 
(cid:131) Image versions
(cid:131) Any-to-Any relation!

(cid:131) CIR is currently IOS feature set independent
(cid:131) CIR successfully tested against IOS 12.0 – 12.5
(cid:131) CIR currently supports 

(cid:131) Cisco 1700 
(cid:131) Cisco 2600
(cid:131) Cisco 3600 (upcoming) 
(cid:131) Cisco 7200 (upcoming)

(cid:131) Your wishes decide the course.

 Summary – Part III

(cid:131) Writing core dumps is a viable method for obtaining 

IOS evidence when it is needed.
(cid:131) The evidence includes forwarded and received packets.
(cid:131) An independent analysis framework can distinguish 
between bugs and attacks, enabling real forensics 
on IOS routers.

(cid:131) Recurity Labs’ CIR already reliably identifies many 

types of attacks and IOS backdoors.
(cid:131) CIR is work-in-progress
(cid:131) CIR’s future depends on the feedback we receive from the 

community.

 Initial Public Offer

(cid:131) An analysis framework’s quality is directly related to 

the amount of cases it has seen
(cid:131) CIR needs a lot more food to grow up
(cid:131) We want to provide it to everyone while constantly 

developing and improving it

(cid:131) Free Service: http://cir.recurity-labs.com

(cid:131) Processing on our servers
(cid:131) Always using the latest version
(cid:131) Please be gentle, it’s the      version

α
(cid:131) Given enough interest, there will be a professional 

tool in the future

 At the end, it’s all up to you!

(cid:131) We think CIR could be useful
(cid:131) For the networking engineer
(cid:131) For the forensics professional
(cid:131) To finally know the state of our infrastructure

(cid:131) We can think of way too many things

(cid:131) Platforms
(cid:131) Features
(cid:131) Reports

(cid:131) Please help ☺

 cir.recurity-labs.com

Felix ´FX´ Lindner
Head

fx@recurity-labs.com

Recurity Labs GmbH, Berlin, Germany
http://www.recurity-labs.com

(cid:131) We need it on-demand (cid:131) We need it when the device crashes
(cid:131) We need an independent and solid analysis
framework to process the evidence (cid:131) We need to be able to extend and adjust it
Getting the Evidence
(cid:131) Cisco IOS can write complete core dumps
(cid:131) Memory dump of the main memory (cid:131) Memory dump of the IO memory (cid:131) Memory dump of the PCI memory (if applicable)
(cid:131) Core dumps are written in two cases
(cid:131) The device crashes (cid:131) The user issues the “write core” command
Core Dump Destinations
(cid:131) IOS supports various destinations
(cid:131) TFTP server (bug!) (cid:131) FTP server (cid:131) RCP server (cid:131) Flash file system (later IOS releases)
(cid:131) Core dumps are enabled by configuration
(cid:131) Configuration commands do not differ between
IOS versions
(cid:131) Configuration change has no effect on the
router’s operation or performance
Core Dump Enabled Infrastructure
(cid:131) Configure all IOS devices to dump core onto one or more centrally located FTP servers (cid:131) Minimizes required monitoring of devices: A router crashed if you find a core dump on the FTP server
(cid:131) Preserves evidence (cid:131) Allows crash correlation between different routers
(cid:131) Why wasn’t it used before?
(cid:131) Core dumps were useless, except for Cisco
developers and exploit writers.
Analyzing Core Dumps
Disclaimer:
(cid:131) Any of the following methods can be
implemented in whatever your preferred programming language is.
(cid:131) This presentation will be centric to our implementation: Recurity Labs CIR.
Core Dump Analyzer Requirements
(cid:131) Must be 100% independent
(cid:131) No Cisco code (cid:131) No disassembly based analysis (cid:131) Must gradually recover abstraction (cid:131) No assumptions about anything (cid:131) Ability to cope with massively corrupted data
(cid:131) Should not be exploitable itself
(cid:131) Preferably not written in C
The Image Blueprint
(cid:131) The IOS image (ELF file) contains all required information about the memory mapping on the router.
(cid:131) The image serves as the memory layout blueprint,
to be applied to the core files
(cid:131) Using a known-to-be-good image also allows verification of the code and read-only data segments (cid:131) Now we can easily and reliably detect runtime
patched images
Heap Reconstruction
(cid:131) IOS uses one large heap (cid:131) The IOS heap contains plenty of meta-data for
debugging purposes (cid:131) 40 bytes overhead per heap block in IOS up to
12.3
(cid:131) 48 bytes overhead per heap block in IOS 12.4
(cid:131) Reconstructing the entire heap allows extensive integrity and validity checks (cid:131) Exceeding by far the on-board checks IOS
performs during runtime
Heap Verification
(cid:131) Full functionality of “CheckHeaps”
(cid:131) Verify the integrity of the allocated and free heap block
doubly linked lists
(cid:131) Find holes in addressable heap
(cid:131) Invisible to CheckHeaps
(cid:131) Identify heap overflow footprints (cid:131) Values not verified by CheckHeaps
(cid:131) Map heap blocks to referencing processes (cid:131) Identify formerly allocated heap blocks
(cid:131) Catches memory usage peaks from the recent past
Process List
(cid:131) Extraction of the IOS Process List (cid:131) Identify the processes’ stack block
(cid:131) Create individual, per process back-traces (cid:131) Identify return address overwrites
(cid:131) Obtain the processes’ scheduling state (cid:131) Obtain the processes’ CPU usage history (cid:131) Obtain the processes’ CPU context
(cid:131) Almost any post mortem analysis method
known can be applied, given the two reconstructed data structures.
TCL Backdoor Detection
(cid:131) TCL scripting is available on later Cisco IOS versions (cid:131) TCL scripts listening on TCP sockets
(cid:131) Well known method (cid:131) Used to simplify automated administration (cid:131) Used to silently keep privileged access to routers (cid:131) Known bug:
not terminated when the VTY session ends (fixed)
(cid:131) Simple TCL backdoor scripts published
(cid:131) CIR can extract all TCP script chunks from IOS heap
and dump them for further analysis
Your Wishes Please !
(cid:131) Interface tables (cid:131) Static routing (cid:131) Router processes (cid:131) VLAN tables (cid:131) VPN context
(cid:131) Keys (cid:131) User (cid:131) IPv6 tables (cid:131) ARP tables (cid:131) Dialer tables
(cid:131) CDP tables (cid:131) Spanning tree (cid:131) Access Lists (cid:131) CEF Tree (cid:131) User sessions (cid:131) Listening ports
(cid:131) Callback code for
incoming connections
(cid:131) Verification that it is located in .TEXT
IOS Packet Forwarding Memory
(cid:131) IOS performs routing either as:
(cid:131) Process switching (cid:131) Fast switching (cid:131) Particle systems (cid:131) Hardware accelerated switching
(cid:131) Except hardware switching, all use IO memory
(cid:131) IO memory is written as separate code dump (cid:131) By default, about 6% of the router’s memory is dedicated
as IO memory
(cid:131) In real world installations, it is common to increase the percentage
to speed up forwarding
(cid:131) Hardware switched packets use PCI memory (cid:131) PCI memory is written as separate core dump
IO Memory Buffers
(cid:131) Routing (switching) ring buffers are grouped by
packet size (cid:131) Small (cid:131) Medium (cid:131) Big (cid:131) Huge
(cid:131) Interfaces have their own buffers for locally handled
traffic
(cid:131) IOS tries really hard to not copy packets around in
memory
(cid:131) New traffic does not automatically erase older traffic
in a linear way
Traffic Extraction
(cid:131) CIR dumps packets that were process switched by
the router from IO memory into a PCAP file (cid:131) Traffic addressed to and from the router itself (cid:131) Traffic that was process switching inspected
(cid:131) Access List matching (cid:131) QoS routed traffic
(cid:131) CIR could dump packets that were forwarded
through the router too (cid:131) Reconstruction of packet fragments possible (cid:131) Is it desirable?
Advanced Traffic Extraction
(cid:131) Writing core to a remote server uses IO memory
(cid:131) Overwrites part of the traffic evidence
(cid:131) CIR can use a GDB link instead of a core dump
(cid:131) Serial GDB protocol allows direct access to router memory
via the console
(cid:131) Uses Zynamics GDB debug link
(cid:131) Disconnecting all network interfaces preserves IO
and PCI memory contents (cid:131) Using GDB halts the router
(cid:131) All data is preserved – useful for emergency
inspections
Traffic Extraction Applications
(cid:131) Identification of attack jump pad routers (cid:131) 0day identification against systems on
segmented network interfaces (cid:131) If you got the packet, you got the 0day
(cid:131) Spoofing attack backtracking (cid:131) One hop at the time, obviously
(cid:131) LE detection
Challenges
(cid:131) The analysis framework has to handle the complexity of the
Cisco IOS landscape (cid:131) Hardware platforms (cid:131) Image versions (cid:131) Any-to-Any relation!
(cid:131) CIR is currently IOS feature set independent (cid:131) CIR successfully tested against IOS 12.0 – 12.5 (cid:131) CIR currently supports
(cid:131) Cisco 1700 (cid:131) Cisco 2600 (cid:131) Cisco 3600 (upcoming) (cid:131) Cisco 7200 (upcoming)
(cid:131) Your wishes decide the course.
Summary – Part III
(cid:131) Writing core dumps is a viable method for obtaining
IOS evidence when it is needed.
(cid:131) The evidence includes forwarded and received packets.
(cid:131) An independent analysis framework can distinguish between bugs and attacks, enabling real forensics on IOS routers.
(cid:131) Recurity Labs’ CIR already reliably identifies many
types of attacks and IOS backdoors.
(cid:131) CIR is work-in-progress (cid:131) CIR’s future depends on the feedback we receive from the
community.
Initial Public Offer

the amount of cases it has seen (cid:131) CIR needs a lot more food to grow up (cid:131) We want to provide it to everyone while constantly
developing and improving it
(cid:131) Free Service: http://cir.recurity-labs.com

α (cid:131) Given enough interest, there will be a professional
tool in the future
At the end, it’s all up to you!

Summary – Part II (cid:131) Identifying compromised routers using today’s tools and methods is hard, if not impossible. (cid:131) There is not enough data to perform any post mortem analysis of router crashes, security related or not. (cid:131) We cannot distinguish between a functional problem, an attempted attack and a successful attack on infrastructure running IOS.
